subtype: Approach: experiment and measure with a small pilot [Action]
passage:
Subject: Pilot results, honest version

Dear Mohit,

You suggested a pilot, so we ran one. Our target was 30 repeat orders in four weeks, counted only from customers who had ordered before. We logged each in one sheet, no rounding up. The final count is 22. We missed. At first it stung, but then we looked at the sheet: 17 of the 22 repeats came from Block B, where we delivered on the same evening every week. Other blocks got random days. So we are treating the miss as a clue, and next month we will fix delivery days everywhere and count again. May we send you the new sheet in four weeks?

Yash

qa.q: How many repeat orders did the team count?
What did Yash feel on seeing that the target was missed?
qa.a: At first it stung, so Yash felt disappointed, but then curious as the sheet pointed to a clue.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the team use if delivery days do not fix it, and why?
qa.a: They could phone a few one-time customers to ask why they did not reorder, because the numbers show what happened but not the reason.

qa.q: How might Mohit see this email?
qa.a: Mohit reads an honest count with the miss stated plainly and a next step, so Mohit can trust the team's numbers and help with the plan.

grounding: Shows a small pilot with a set target, an honest count, and treating a missed target as useful information.

subtype: Approach: experiment and measure with a small pilot [Action]
passage: Aditi, you asked how our tiffin pilot went. Honestly? We missed. I'm Saurabh, and I'll give you the numbers, because we promised ourselves we would. The goal for October was thirty repeat orders: people who ordered once and came back. We didn't count first orders, because friends order once to be nice. We kept a sheet, and every Sunday we counted, no rounding up. Week one: four. Week two: six. Week three: five. Week four: four. Nineteen. Not thirty. For about an hour I sulked. Then we looked at who came back. Almost all were students in the far hostel, where the mess is terrible. Nobody from the near hostel came back at all. So the target wasn't an insult. It told us where the real customers are. November's pilot: only the far hostel, same target.

qa.q: How many repeat orders did they get?
How did Saurabh feel on missing the target?
qa.a: Saurabh felt sulky and disappointed for about an hour, before seeing the useful pattern in the numbers.

qa.q: What else could they measure in November?
qa.a: They could ask the repeat customers why they came back and track which dishes get reordered, so the pilot teaches even more.

qa.q: How might Aditi see Saurabh's honesty about the miss?
qa.a: Aditi hears a clear, honest account, which likely makes the lesson about the far hostel easy to trust.

grounding: Shows a team setting a target of thirty repeat orders in a month, counting honestly, and treating the miss as information about real customers.

subtype: Approach: experiment and measure with a small pilot [Action]
passage: I'm Shalini, Deepak's lab partner, and I watched his pilot from the next bench all through March. His team was testing a service that takes hostel students' files to the city print shop and delivers the printouts by evening. The target was on a sticky note on his laptop: "Thirty repeat orders by 31 March." Every Saturday he counted out loud and wouldn't let his cofounder round up. "Seven. Not ten, seven." On the 31st the total was twenty-two. I expected him to be crushed. He sat quietly for a minute, then started sorting the sheet by department. "Look. Architecture students placed nine of these. They print huge drawings every week." He stuck a new note on the laptop: "April: architecture only. Thirty." I don't know if he was hurt. He didn't show it.

qa.q: What was the total on the 31st?
What might Deepak have felt on seeing twenty-two?
qa.a: Deepak may have felt disappointed, sitting quietly for a minute, but quickly turned curious about who the orders came from.

qa.q: What else could Deepak's team try in April?
qa.a: They could talk to a few architecture students about their printing needs, so the service fits them even better.

qa.q: How does Shalini see Deepak's reaction?
qa.a: Shalini expected Deepak to be crushed but watches him treat the miss as information, without being sure what he felt inside.

grounding: Illustrates a team counting repeat orders honestly against a monthly target of thirty and treating the shortfall as information, not an insult.
